\section[a catástrofe]{a catástrofe — the catastrophe}

\label{lesson:PT-C304-catastrofe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the alert, then the Portuguese for to warn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a catástrofe}
\textbf{a catástrofe} — \textquotedblleft{}the catastrophe\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O sismo foi uma catástrofe para a região.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The quake was a catastrophe for the region.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Uma catástrofe natural} — a natural disaster.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{catástrofe} comes from Greek \emph{katastroph\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}an overturning, a sudden end\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{katastréphein} \textquotedblleft{}to turn down\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{stréphein} \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a catástrofe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a catástrofe}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a catástrofe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the alert, then the Portuguese for to warn, then say \emph{a catástrofe} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a catástrofe mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The catastrophe\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o desastre]{o desastre — the disaster; a crash}

\label{lesson:PT-C304-desastre}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to warn, then the Portuguese for the catastrophe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o desastre}
\textbf{o desastre} — \textquotedblleft{}the disaster; a crash\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O jogo foi um desastre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The match was a disaster.}
\end{quote}

Also a road crash: \emph{um desastre de carro}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desastre} came through Middle French from Italian \emph{disastro} \textquotedblleft{}an ill-starred event\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{astro} \textquotedblleft{}a star\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{astrum}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o desastre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o desastre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o desastre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to warn, then the Portuguese for the catastrophe, then say \emph{o desastre} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[a tragédia]{a tragédia — the tragedy}

\label{lesson:PT-C304-tragedia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the catastrophe, then the Portuguese for the disaster.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a tragédia}
\textbf{a tragédia} — \textquotedblleft{}the tragedy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A morte do jovem foi uma tragédia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The young man’s death was a tragedy.}
\end{quote}

Also the kind of play.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tragédia} was borrowed from Latin \emph{tragoedia} (EtymDB), from Greek \emph{tragōidía}, built on \emph{trágos} \textquotedblleft{}a goat\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ōid\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}a song\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o deslizamento]{o deslizamento — the landslide; a slip}

\label{lesson:PT-C304-deslizamento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the disaster, then the Portuguese for the tragedy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o deslizamento}
\textbf{o deslizamento} — \textquotedblleft{}the landslide; a slip\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Um deslizamento de terra cortou a estrada.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A landslide cut the road.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Deslizamento de terras} — landslide.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{deslizamento} is built on \emph{deslizar} \textquotedblleft{}to slide\textquotedblright{} with the ending \emph{-mento}; the origin of the verb is not settled, and EtymDB has no entry.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[soterrar]{soterrar — to bury under earth or rubble}

\label{lesson:PT-C304-soterrar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the tragedy, then the Portuguese for the landslide.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: soterrar}
\textbf{soterrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to bury under earth or rubble\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A lama soterrou duas casas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The mud buried two houses.}
\end{quote}

Mostly of disasters: mud, snow or rubble.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{soterrar} is built on \emph{terra} \textquotedblleft{}earth\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{terra}, with \emph{so-} \textquotedblleft{}under\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
